lessons.title: Common Duck Diseases and Symptoms
lessons.body:
Ducks are hardy but can fall sick quickly. Learn to spot the early signs: a duck that separates from the flock, sits hunched, refuses feed, or has watery eyes and a dirty vent. Common diseases in Africa include Duck Viral Hepatitis (DVH), Duck Plague (Duck Viral Enteritis), Avian Influenza (Bird Flu), Botulism, and Aspergillosis. DVH kills young ducklings fast, often within 24 hours, with symptoms like spasms and head retraction. Duck Plague causes sudden death, bloody diarrhea, and swollen eyelids. Avian Influenza brings high fever, swollen head, and sudden death; it is a zoonotic disease, so report it to authorities immediately. Botulism comes from eating spoiled food or dead animals in stagnant water; ducks become paralyzed, starting with the legs, then neck (limberneck). Aspergillosis is a fungal infection from moldy feed or bedding; symptoms include gasping, sneezing, and weight loss.

To diagnose, observe your flock twice daily. Look for changes in behavior, appetite, and droppings. A healthy duck has bright eyes, clean feathers, and stands upright. Sick ducks may have greenish or bloody droppings. For bacterial diseases like fowl cholera, you may see swollen joints and difficulty breathing. Viral diseases often have no cure, so prevention is key. If you suspect a disease, isolate the sick duck immediately in a separate pen with clean water and feed. Wear gloves and wash hands after handling. Do not sell or eat sick birds. Call a vet or extension officer for confirmation. In many African countries, you can contact the local veterinary department for free or low-cost diagnosis. Early action saves the flock.

Keep records: note the date, symptoms, number affected, and deaths. This helps the vet identify patterns. For example, if ducklings die suddenly with opisthotonus (head pulled back), suspect DVH. If adult ducks die after swimming in a stagnant pond, suspect botulism. Remember, many diseases spread through contaminated water, feed, and equipment. Clean and disinfect drinkers and feeders daily. Avoid mixing ducks with other poultry, especially chickens, as they can carry diseases like avian influenza without showing symptoms. Vaccinate where possible (see Lesson 2). Your quick response can mean the difference between losing a few birds and losing your entire flock.

lessons.title: Vaccination and Deworming Protocols
lessons.body:
Vaccination is your best defense against killer diseases. For ducks, the core vaccines are Duck Viral Hepatitis (DVH) and Duck Plague (Duck Viral Enteritis). In many African countries, these vaccines are available from veterinary supply stores or government extension offices. DVH vaccine is given to ducklings at 1-2 weeks of age, often as a shot under the wing (subcutaneous) or in the breast muscle. A booster is given 2-4 weeks later. For Duck Plague, vaccinate at 3-4 weeks old, then annually. If you keep breeders, vaccinate them 2-4 weeks before laying so chicks get maternal immunity. Note: Avian Influenza vaccine is not commonly used in ducks in Africa due to trade restrictions; instead, focus on biosecurity. Always buy vaccines from a reputable source and check the expiry date. Keep vaccines cold (2-8Â°C) using a cooler with ice packs during transport. Use a new needle for each bird or disinfect between birds with 70% alcohol to avoid spreading disease.

Deworming: Ducks get internal parasites like roundworms, tapeworms, and gizzard worms. Deworm every 3-4 months with a poultry dewormer such as piperazine, levamisole, or albendazole. Dosage: piperazine is often given in water at 100 mg per kg body weight for one day, repeated after 2 weeks. Levamisole: 20-30 mg/kg orally. Albendazole: 10-20 mg/kg orally for 3 days. For external parasites like lice and mites, use ivermectin at 0.2 mg/kg injected under the skin, repeated after 10 days. Alternatively, dust with diatomaceous earth or use permethrin powder. Always follow label instructions and withdraw eggs for the recommended period (e.g., 7 days for most dewormers).

Create a health calendar: Month 1: DVH vaccine at week 1 and 3. Month 2: Duck Plague vaccine at week 4. Month 3: first deworming. Then repeat deworming every 3 months. Keep a notebook with dates, products used, and batch numbers. If you see tapeworm segments in droppings (white, flat, moving), deworm immediately. For coccidiosis (bloody droppings), use amprolium in water for 5 days. Remember, vaccines only work if ducks are healthy; do not vaccinate sick birds. Also, avoid vaccinating during extreme heat stress. If you are unsure, consult a vet or experienced duck farmer in your area. Many African farmers share vaccines to reduce costs, but never share needles without sterilizing.

lessons.title: Biosecurity Measures on the Farm
lessons.body:
Biosecurity means keeping germs out and stopping them from spreading. On a duck farm, start with a fence to keep wild birds, rodents, and strangers out. Wild ducks and waterfowl carry avian influenza and duck plague. If your ducks free-range near a pond, they can catch diseases from wild birds. Ideally, keep your ducks in a covered run with a roof and wire mesh sides. Use a footbath at the entrance of each pen: a shallow tray with disinfectant (e.g., 2% sodium hypochlorite or quaternary ammonium). Change the disinfectant daily. Wear dedicated boots and overalls only inside the farm. Do not let visitors enter pens unless necessary; if they must, give them clean boots and a lab coat.

Clean water is critical. Ducks foul water quickly. Use nipple drinkers or troughs that are easy to empty and scrub. Empty and refill drinkers at least twice a day. Once a week, scrub with a brush and disinfectant, then rinse well. Feeders should be raised off the ground to prevent contamination with droppings. Store feed in sealed containers away from rodents. Never feed moldy or spoiled feedâit causes aspergillosis and botulism. Remove dead ducks immediately; bury them deep (1 meter) with lime or burn them. Do not throw carcasses into the bush or water.

All-in, all-out management works best: raise one batch of ducks at a time, then clean and disinfect the pen thoroughly before bringing new birds. If you must add new ducks, quarantine them for 30 days in a separate area. Watch for symptoms. After handling sick birds, change clothes and wash hands with soap. Keep a separate set of tools for sick pens. Control flies and mosquitoes with screens and traps; they spread fowl pox and other diseases. Finally, keep records of all visitors, new birds, and deaths. This helps trace disease outbreaks. In Africa, many farmers share equipment; avoid borrowing or lending nets, feeders, or boots without disinfecting. A simple biosecurity routine can cut disease by 80%.

lessons.title: Parasite Control: Internal and External
lessons.body:
Parasites steal nutrients, reduce egg production, and can kill young ducks. Internal parasites include roundworms (Ascaridia), tapeworms (Raillietina), gizzard worms (Amidostomum), and coccidia (Eimeria). Symptoms: weight loss, pale comb, diarrhea, and seeing worms in droppings. Deworm regularly: every 3 months for adults, every 6 weeks for growing ducks. Use piperazine (100 mg/kg in water for 1 day), levamisole (20-30 mg/kg orally), or albendazole (10-20 mg/kg orally for 3 days). For coccidiosis, use amprolium (1 g per 2 liters of water for 5 days). Rotate dewormers to prevent resistance. After deworming, collect droppings and burn them; do not use as fertilizer for 2 weeks.

External parasites: lice, mites, fleas, and ticks. Lice are pale and move slowly on feathers; mites are tiny and cause crusty skin, especially around the vent and under wings. Ducks infested with mites become restless, lose weight, and may stop laying. Treat with ivermectin injection (0.2 mg/kg under the skin, repeat after 10 days). Alternatively, dust ducks with permethrin powder or diatomaceous earth, focusing on the vent, under wings, and neck. For severe lice, use a 0.5% malathion dust. Treat the pen too: spray with permethrin or sprinkle diatomaceous earth on bedding. Clean nest boxes and replace bedding weekly. Sun-drying bedding kills mites.

Prevention: Keep the pen dry. Ducks love water but wet litter breeds parasites. Provide a shallow water bath for swimming, but change it daily and keep the area around it drained. Avoid overcrowding: allow at least 1 square meter per duck in the pen. Rotate grazing areas if you free-range. Plant herbs like garlic, neem, and wormwood around the pen; some farmers feed crushed neem leaves (1 teaspoon per duck per week) as a natural dewormer, but this is not a substitute for proper medication. Quarantine new birds for 30 days and treat them for parasites before mixing. Check your ducks weekly: part feathers and look at the skin. If you see moving specks or scabs, treat immediately. Remember, parasites spread fast, so act on the first sign.

lessons.title: First Aid and Treating Injuries
lessons.body:
Ducks get injured from predators, sharp objects, or fighting. Keep a first aid kit: clean cloth, antiseptic (povidone-iodine), antibiotic ointment, gauze, vet wrap, scissors, tweezers, and saline solution. For a cut or scrape, wash with saline or clean water, apply antiseptic, then cover with gauze and vet wrap. Change daily. If bleeding heavily, apply pressure with a clean cloth for 5 minutes. For a broken leg, splint with a small stick and vet wrap, keeping the leg straight. Isolate the duck in a small, quiet pen with soft bedding. Limit movement for 2 weeks. For a broken wing, wrap the wing against the body with vet wrap, but do not wrap too tight. Check circulation. Most wing fractures heal in 3-4 weeks.

Bumblefoot is a common foot infection: a swollen, black scab on the foot pad. Soak the foot in warm salt water (1 teaspoon per liter) for 10 minutes twice daily. Apply antibiotic ointment and bandage. If not improved in 3 days, see a vet for antibiotics. For eye injuries, flush with saline and apply terramycin eye ointment. For poisoning (e.g., botulism or lead), give activated charcoal (1 g per kg) mixed in water, and keep the duck warm and quiet. There is no antidote for botulism; supportive care may save mild cases. For heat stress, move ducks to shade, provide cool water, and dip their feet in cool water. For frostbite (rare in Africa but possible in highlands), warm the area gradually with lukewarm waterânever hot.

After any injury, keep the duck separate but within sight of the flock to reduce stress. Provide easy access to feed and water. Use a shallow dish to prevent drowning if the duck is weak. If the duck is not eating, try offering mashed boiled egg or soft porridge. Administer electrolytes in water (e.g., 1 teaspoon salt, 1 teaspoon sugar per liter). Always wash your hands before and after treating. If an injury is severe (deep wound, exposed bone, or maggots), call a vet. Maggots can be removed with tweezers and the wound flushed with hydrogen peroxide diluted 1:1 with water. Do not use human painkillers like ibuprofen or paracetamolâthey are toxic to ducks. With prompt care, most ducks recover quickly.

lessons.title: Working with a Veterinarian
lessons.body:
A good veterinarian is your partner in keeping ducks healthy. In Africa, find a vet who treats poultry or has experience with waterfowl. Contact your local veterinary department, agricultural extension office, or a nearby veterinary college. Some vets specialize in poultry; ask if they have worked with ducks. Establish a relationship before an emergency. Invite the vet to your farm for a routine visit once or twice a year. They can check overall health, advise on vaccination schedules, and inspect biosecurity. A farm visit may cost $20-50, but it can save you hundreds in losses. If you cannot afford a vet, look for community animal health workers or experienced duck farmers who can mentor you.

When a disease outbreak occurs, call the vet immediately. Describe symptoms: number sick, number dead, age, and any recent changes (new feed, new birds, weather). If the vet cannot come, they may ask you to bring a sick duck or a dead one for post-mortem. For post-mortem, wrap the dead duck in a plastic bag and keep it cool (not frozen) until delivery. Never open a dead duck yourself unless trainedâyou could spread disease. The vet may take samples (blood, swabs, organs) and send them to a lab. In many countries, government labs test for avian influenza and Newcastle disease for free. Results may take 1-2 weeks. Meanwhile, isolate sick birds and disinfect.

Follow the vet's instructions exactly. If they prescribe antibiotics, complete the full course even if ducks look better. Withdrawal periods for meat and eggs: for example, oxytetracycline has a 5-day meat withdrawal and 7-day egg withdrawal. Record all treatments. If the vet recommends culling, do it humanely: use a sharp knife to sever the jugular vein or use a captive bolt. Bury deep with lime. Do not sell sick ducks. After an outbreak, work with the vet to review biosecurity and vaccination. Ask for a written health plan. Keep the vet's phone number handy. In remote areas, you can use mobile phones to send photos of symptoms to a vet for advice. Many African vets now offer teleconsultation. Remember, a vet is not just for emergenciesâregular check-ups keep your flock productive and profitable.

quiz.q: Which disease causes ducklings to die suddenly with head retraction and spasms?
quiz.explanation: Duck Viral Hepatitis primarily affects young ducklings and causes sudden death with neurological signs like head retraction.

quiz.q: What is a common symptom of botulism in ducks?
options: B) Paralysis starting in the legs
quiz.explanation: Botulism causes flaccid paralysis, often starting with the legs and progressing to the neck (limberneck).

quiz.q: Which disease is zoonotic and must be reported to authorities?
quiz.explanation: Avian Influenza can infect humans and is a notifiable disease in most countries.

quiz.q: What is the recommended age for the first Duck Viral Hepatitis vaccine?
quiz.explanation: DVH vaccine is given early, typically at 1-2 weeks of age, to protect vulnerable ducklings.

quiz.q: How often should you deworm adult ducks?
quiz.explanation: Regular deworming every 3-4 months prevents internal parasite buildup.

quiz.q: Which dewormer is given in water at 100 mg/kg for one day?
quiz.explanation: Piperazine is commonly administered in drinking water for one day to treat roundworms.

quiz.q: What is the withdrawal period for eggs after most dewormers?
quiz.explanation: Most dewormers require a 7-day egg withdrawal to ensure residues are cleared.

quiz.q: Which biosecurity measure helps prevent wild birds from spreading disease?
options: B) Covering the run with wire mesh
quiz.explanation: Covering the run with wire mesh keeps wild birds out, reducing disease transmission.

quiz.q: How often should you change the disinfectant in a footbath?
quiz.explanation: Disinfectant loses potency quickly, so it should be changed daily.

quiz.q: What is the ideal quarantine period for new ducks?
quiz.explanation: A 30-day quarantine allows time for any latent diseases to show.

quiz.q: Which internal parasite causes weight loss and pale comb?
quiz.explanation: Roundworms compete for nutrients, leading to weight loss and anemia (pale comb).

quiz.q: What is the treatment for coccidiosis in ducks?
quiz.explanation: Amprolium is effective against coccidia and is given in water for 5 days.

quiz.q: Which external parasite causes crusty skin around the vent?
quiz.explanation: Mites burrow into the skin, causing crusts and irritation, especially around the vent.

quiz.q: How is ivermectin administered for external parasites?
quiz.explanation: Ivermectin is given by subcutaneous injection at 0.2 mg/kg, repeated after 10 days.

quiz.q: What is a natural remedy sometimes used to deter parasites?
quiz.explanation: Garlic has some antiparasitic properties, though not as effective as medication.

quiz.q: What is the first step in treating a bleeding wound on a duck?
options: B) Apply pressure with a clean cloth
quiz.explanation: Applying pressure helps stop bleeding before further treatment.

quiz.q: How should you treat bumblefoot?
options: A) Soak in warm salt water
quiz.explanation: Soaking in warm salt water softens the scab and helps healing; antibiotics may be needed if severe.

quiz.q: What is the correct dilution of hydrogen peroxide for flushing maggot wounds?
quiz.explanation: A 1:1 dilution with water is safe for flushing wounds; undiluted can damage tissue.

quiz.q: Which human painkiller is toxic to ducks?
quiz.explanation: Ibuprofen and paracetamol are toxic to ducks and should never be used.

quiz.q: What should you do if a duck has a broken leg?
options: A) Splint it with a stick
B) Let it heal on its own
quiz.explanation: Splinting with a stick and vet wrap keeps the leg aligned for healing.

quiz.q: What is the role of a veterinarian in duck farming?
options: C) To provide routine health checks and advice
quiz.explanation: Vets help with preventive care, diagnosis, and treatment, not just emergencies.

quiz.q: How should you prepare a dead duck for post-mortem?
options: B) Keep it cool and wrap in plastic
C) Leave it in the sun
quiz.explanation: Keeping the carcass cool (not frozen) and wrapped preserves tissues for accurate diagnosis.

quiz.q: What is a common withdrawal period for oxytetracycline in eggs?
quiz.explanation: Oxytetracycline typically requires a 7-day egg withdrawal to avoid residues.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of a sick duck?
quiz.explanation: A hunched posture indicates illness or pain; healthy ducks stand upright.

quiz.q: What should you do with dead ducks after a disease outbreak?
quiz.explanation: Deep burial with lime prevents scavengers and spread of disease.

quiz.q: Which vaccine is given at 3-4 weeks old and then annually?
quiz.explanation: Duck Plague vaccine is administered at 3-4 weeks and boosted annually.

quiz.q: What is the recommended dosage of piperazine for deworming?
quiz.explanation: Piperazine is given at 100 mg per kg body weight in water for one day.

quiz.q: How can you prevent aspergillosis?
options: B) Store feed in dry, sealed containers
D) Keep ducks in dark, damp pens
quiz.explanation: Aspergillosis is caused by moldy feed or bedding, so dry storage prevents it.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to do when you suspect a disease outbreak?
quiz.explanation: Isolating sick birds immediately helps prevent the spread of disease to healthy flock members.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good biosecurity practice?
options: B) Allowing visitors into pens freely
C) Using a footbath at entry
quiz.explanation: A footbath disinfects boots and reduces the risk of introducing pathogens.
